Notes: Liebermann: Once belonging to Worcester cathedral priory, mainly canon-law and theological extracts, largely Latin; contains IV Edgar in Latin version and in English, and an excommunication formula against despisers of God's law. Wormald: Corpus 265 is a mid-eleventh-century Worcester compendium of canon law, penitential and liturgical texts for a working bishop, whose first part is among the most systematic surviving forms of the canon collection associated with Archbishop Wulfstan. Its separate second section contains IV Edgar, uniquely in both Latin and Old English, set between formulae for excommunicating and absolving enemies of the Church and the Maundy Thursday rite for reconciling penitents — a placing Wormald explains by the code's insistence on tithe. The Latin version, he suggests, was made so that a royal code could take its place in a learned Latin collection of church law, and a related twelfth-century collection (Barlow 37) hints that IV Edgar may have belonged to the collection from an early stage.

Its separate second section contains IV Edgar, uniquely in both Latin and Old English, set between formulae for excommunicating and absolving enemies of the Church and the Maundy Thursday rite for reconciling penitents — a placing Wormald explains by the code's insistence on tithe. The Latin version, he suggests, was made so that a royal code could take its place in a learned Latin collection of church law, and a related twelfth-century collection (Barlow 37) hints that IV Edgar may have belonged to the collection from an early stage.

Notes: Liebermann: The York Minster gospel book (c. 1025), followed by homilies of c. 1030–70 repeating passages from Æthelred and Cnut, then in the same hand on a flyleaf Cnut's letter of 1020. Notes: [not in Liebermann] Wormald: A copy in the Bodleian of Lambarde's Archaionomia, as reissued by Whelock, in which Richard Taylor entered, in 1811, the readings of a now-lost twelfth-century parchment leaf of II–III Edgar that he had seen at Norwich, apparently adding a careful facsimile of it. The leaf seems to have been a plain copy in long lines, probably not from a luxury MS, perhaps from one of the twelfth-century legal compilations or a stand-alone copy like Harley 55(B). Its text, like those of Nero A.i(A) and Quadripartitus, lacks the variants of the Wulfstan manuscripts, and it is further evidence both of interest in Old English law under Henry II and of the circulation of the major codes in differing versions.
